segments.text: There is a difference between an activity and an experience, and it is not
vocabulary. An activity is something the guests did.
An experience is something they take away.
The same harvest at 5:00 in the afternoon with the same people can be either.
And what decides? It is not the script or the equipment. It is how it is led.
This model gives you the tool to decide that on purpose, not by luck.
The tool has four registers from research into the experience economy.
Any moment you offer lives in four dimensions.
Aesthetic, the guest is somewhere beautiful and needs to do nothing.
Educational, they learn something new.
Escapist, they take part, they choose, they get their hands dirty.
Entertainment, they enjoy themselves, they laugh.
Memorable experiences touch all four. Weak ones stay in one.
And most badly designed activities get stuck in the educational, someone explaining
things to people standing still. Apply it to the harvest, our most common
experience. Aesthetic, arriving at the garden late in the afternoon and just being
there because the light does the work. Do not fill it with information.
Educational, one thing, one only, that they did not know.
Why this courgette exists in August and not January.
Escapist, they cut, they pick, they choose.
If they only watch, it is a demonstration.
Entertainment, something that makes them laugh.
The hen that follows them, the child who finds an egg.
Second rule, choice instead of a program.
The value a guest puts on an experience rises when they help decide what to do, not
only do it. In practice, a different sentence.
Instead of, "Tomorrow at 10:00, there is a harvest," we say,
"Tomorrow there is a harvest at 10:00, and bread at 5:00. Both one.
Or would you rather keep the morning free?" The option of doing nothing has to be
on the table set by us. That makes the rest an invitation, not a timetable.
Third rule, the first 90 seconds. Arrival sets the expectation for the whole stay.
The only moment with no second chance. The standard.
Recognized by name, take the bag, offer water, drop the pace immediately.
We do not check in at the counter if we can avoid it. We walk and talk.
One or two real questions. "First time with us?
Anything we should know to make this better?" And we listen to the answer.
Ninety seconds done well. By margin for three days.
Fourth rule, the peak and the end. Memory forms at the peak and at the end,
not on the average. Two consequences. One, guarantee a deliberate peak per stay.
Dinner under the stars, the sauna at dusk, bread out of the oven.
A stay can be entirely correct and have no peak, and no peak means no
recommendation. Two, the goodbye can never be the weakest
moment. A rushed departure wipes out three good days.
A genuine farewell, help with the luggage, a small gesture from the farm, an
invitation to return that does not sound commercial.
Fifth rule, whoever leads has to know the land, not the script.
An experience led by someone who memorized a text is obvious within 30 seconds.
Led by someone who knows what goes on here, it takes any question and survives the
rain, the delay, the difficult group.
And when a guest asks something you cannot answer, which will happen, do not
invent. Take them to someone who knows, then learn the answer for next time.
That is not failure. Inventing is.
And the last, cross-recommendation is hospitality, not selling.
Sending a guest from the pool to the beach bar, or a couple who love dinner into a
conversation about weddings, takes them to more of what they already chose.
The practical distinction, recommend what you would recommend to a friend, and stop
at the first hesitation. Five rules then.
The four registers, choice instead of a program, 90 seconds, peak and
end, and whoever leads knows the land.
Last module, wellbeing, guest, and team.
And what to do when something goes wrong.
